HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded answer):
The gardening pathway shows its distinct prevalence style in low-elevation, human-modified and water-associated habitats — specifically Urban, Riparian, Wetlands and Coastal — where it is simultaneously (i) the dominant or near-dominant introduction pathway among non-native species and (ii) spatially common across plots. In Urban plots 31/65 (47.7%) host ≥1 gardening-introduced non-native species (the highest absolute load: 45 gardening species occurrences), in Wetlands gardening accounts for 55.8% of all non-native species occurrences (19/38 plots affected), in Coastal 53.5% (13/29 plots), and in Riparian 36.5% with the closest stream proximity (median 65 m; 22/61 plots). By contrast, in Croplands the unintentional pathway dominates (gardening share only 18.5%, 20 vs 88 occurrences), and in natural/forested habitats (broad-leaved and coniferous forests, rock outcrops) non-native species are so rare (13 occurrences in 202 plots) that gardening is effectively absent despite a nominally high share (0.846) on a tiny denominator. The habitat differences are highly significant (gardening-vs-other χ²=45.2, df=7, p=1.2e-07; permutation p=0.0001; full 3-pathway χ²=70.3, df=14, p=1.7e-09), and a logistic model of plot-level gardening presence (117/632 events) shows Urban (OR 10.6), Wetlands (9.4), Riparian (8.9) and Coastal (7.6) plots remain 8–11× more likely than natural/forested plots to host gardening species after adjusting for landscape covariates, with lower elevation an independent factor (OR 0.82 per 100 m, p=8e-04). These habitats are distinguished by low median elevation (10–378 m vs 591–990 m in forests/rock), high urban land cover (Urban: 95% urban within 50 m), proximity to streams/roads, and recent landscape change — the contextual signature of gardens, ornamental planting and disturbed, moist, human-adjacent edges. This is consistent with gardening being a recent, human-driven pathway (75.2% of all introductions occurred 1985–2019, vs 16.8% before 1500), which preferentially establishes where human infrastructure and modified, low-elevation, riparian/coastal settings concentrate.

Differences across habitats are highly significant (χ²=45.2, df=7, p=1.2e-07; permutation p=0.0001); logistic models show Urban (OR 10.6), Wetlands (9.4), Riparian (8.9) and Coastal (7.6) plots remain 8–11× more likely than natural/forested plots to host gardening-introduced species after landscape adjustment, with lower elevation (OR 0.82 per 100 m) an independent factor. The distinguishing context is human modification and proximity to water at low elevation — high urban land cover (95% within 50 m in Urban plots), stream/road proximity, low median elevation (10–378 m vs 591–990 m in forests/rock) and recent landscape change — matching the signature of gardens, ornamental planting and disturbed moist, human-adjacent edges; this is consistent with gardening being a recent, human-driven pathway (75.2% of all introductions 1985–2019 vs 16.8% before 1500).
payload.workflow: (1) Loaded data/invaded_niche_pathways.csv (632 plots, tab-separated, no NAs); verified n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo=n.total in all rows. (2) Computed per-habitat table: plot counts, plots with n.gard>0, Σn.gard, Σn.total, gardening share with Wilson 95% CIs, mean n.gard per plot and per positive plot. (3) Tested habitat differences: χ² on gardening-vs-other contingency (sparse natural/forested habitats pooled, Σn.total≤8), validated with a 10,000-iteration margin-fixing permutation test; focused 2×2 Fisher test (human-modified vs agricultural/natural); full 3-pathway×habitat χ². (4) Descriptive landscape context by habitat (medians/IQR for elevation, urban/cropland % 2009, progressive change 1956–2009, distance to stream/road, climate). (5) Logistic regression of plot-level gardening presence (117/632 events) on habitat groups (ref: Natural/forested) and on habitat + 5 landscape covariates (statsmodels). (6) Corroboration from temporal_trends_contingency_table.csv (gardening share by introduction period) and invasion_success_pathways.csv (42/81 species Gardening). All steps in analysis.py; outputs in results_full_output.txt and results_table1_habitat.csv.
